issues.issue: The guarantee excludes PRODUCTS "manufactured by DISTRIBUTOR and shipped under DISTRIBUTOR'S labels," a situation impossible under Section 1(ii), which defines PRODUCTS as goods COMPANY authorizes for sale to DISTRIBUTOR. The carve-out cannot be given effect consistently with the definition and invites argument about what it covers.

The clause says COMPANY "shall supply" the listed information and materials but qualifies it "at COMPANY'S sole discretion" and "as may be available," so it is unclear whether any obligation exists at all. "Commercial product literature in reasonable quantities" supplies no measurable standard either.

DISTRIBUTOR is barred from using any advertising or descriptive literature pertaining to PRODUCTS without prior written consent, while Section 3(ii)(v) makes DISTRIBUTOR "solely responsible for any and all promotions, sales and marketing programs, advertising and the like." Which provision governs distributor-generated promotion would have to be construed.

"General market information regarding the TERRITORY" is undefined and unbounded, giving no way to tell what DISTRIBUTOR must produce on request. The obligation also sits oddly with the confidentiality of DISTRIBUTOR's own customer data.

The confidentiality obligation covers "any and all business and technical information pertaining to the COMPANY and/or the PRODUCTS" with no carve-out for publicly known or independently obtained information and no time limit. What information is captured, and for how long, is left to argument.

Section 12(i) permits termination on ninety days' notice only "for good cause" or on a change in COMPANY's business, which cannot be squared with Section 2's provision that the Agreement continues "until either party terminates ... by providing ... written notice of termination at least ninety (90) days prior." Whether termination without cause was available is the central construction question.

This subsection allows COMPANY to terminate "immediately" for the listed events, while Section 12(i) states that the Agreement may be terminated "by either party at any time upon ninety (90) days written notice ... for good cause." Whether a listed event permits immediate termination or still requires ninety days' notice is unresolved on the face of Section 12.

The five-business-day notice and cure mechanism for non-payment and out-of-channel selling cannot be squared with Section 12(i), which conditions termination for "good cause" on ninety days' written notice. Which notice period a terminating COMPANY must observe is a question the two provisions leave open.

The catch-all covers any failure "which, in the sole discretion of COMPANY, are material," leaving materiality wholly to the terminating party, and pairs a five-day cure period with an undefined "longer, commercially reasonable period" for breaches not curable in five days. Which category a given default falls into, and how long the cure period then runs, is indeterminate.

The repurchase option is at COMPANY's option and at "DISTRIBUTOR'S net warehouse cost," a figure the Agreement nowhere defines, and the sentence closes with a stray "for.)." What DISTRIBUTOR is entitled to receive for remaining inventory on termination is therefore uncertain.

The sentence bars liability for "consequential, punitive or incidental damages ... in any cumulative amount greater than the sum of 50% of DISTRIBUTOR'S aggregate gross sales" in the preceding twelve months, so it is unclear whether the 50% figure is a cap on all damages or only on the excluded categories. It is also unclear whether an exclusion and a cap can coexist, since damages of the listed kinds appear both barred and permitted up to the cap.

The security interest and irrevocable self-help entry right extend to "all PRODUCTS and related items ... in DISTRIBUTOR'S possession," including goods already sold to DISTRIBUTOR absolutely with title passing under Section 4(iii). Whether COMPANY may repossess goods it no longer owns, and without notice, would have to be construed against that provision.

The two-year period runs from when "the harm that gave rise to the cause of action arose," which is not the same as accrual and may precede the claimant's knowledge of it. When the clock starts for a continuing course of conduct, such as ongoing under-delivery or territorial encroachment, is left open.

The mutual indemnity covers claims "caused or alleged to be caused, by a breach of this Agreement by" the indemnifying party, without saying whether it reaches first-party claims between COMPANY and DISTRIBUTOR or only third-party claims. Read the first way it would let a party recover its attorneys' fees for the other's breach.

The clause opens by requiring "each party" to maintain the listed coverage, but the enumerated policies and the certificate obligation are drawn for DISTRIBUTOR alone and only DISTRIBUTOR must furnish evidence. Whether COMPANY owes any of these coverages, or must name DISTRIBUTOR as an additional insured in practice, is unclear.

COMPANY is given the right "in its sole discretion, to inspect, copy, and audit all such records" while the same sentence limits access to records of "services performed for COMPANY." The two halves of the sentence describe different scopes of audit.

The clause lists personal service, facsimile, overnight courier and registered mail as permitted methods, but then fixes the effective date of notice only for mail or facsimile, saying nothing about courier or personal delivery. When a ninety-day termination notice under Section 12(i) becomes effective can turn on that gap.

The clause states that DISTRIBUTOR "shall not have the right or power to assign" and that any attempted assignment is "void," yet in the next paragraph promises that COMPANY "will not unreasonably withhold or delay consent," and it uses the undefined pronouns "our" and "we" for COMPANY. Whether consent may be refused at will or only reasonably is unresolved on the face of the provision.

The requirement that modifications be made only "by a written instrument duly executed by the parties" cannot be squared with Section 3(ii)(c), which lets COMPANY revise Exhibit B unilaterally and "without notice," or with Section 3(ii)(b) and Section 4's unilateral changes to policies and prices. A court would have to decide whether such unilateral changes are effective amendments.

The merger clause "wholly cancels, voids, and supersedes any agreement heretofore entered into between the parties with respect to the subject matter hereof," which puts in issue whether the parties' April 23, 2008 DSDD Distributor Agreement, and rights accrued under it, survive. The qualifier "except as otherwise expressly provided herein" is not tied to any identified surviving provision.

The territory is filled in by hand as "Py, N'T) PA, Cann.," an entry that is partly illegible and does not identify the geographic boundaries with any precision. Since Section 1(iii) defines TERRITORY solely by reference to this exhibit, the scope of the grant is indeterminate on the face of the instrument.

The exclusion list is built of open-ended categories such as "Specialty stores (including airport stores and military exchange stores)," "Chain Warehouse programs" and "value discount stores," none of which is defined and several of which could capture grocery outlets. Whether a given account falls inside an excluded category, and hence outside the authorized channel, is left to argument.

This grandfather clause permits continued sales to excluded-channel customers "as of the date hereof," which cannot be squared with Section 3(ii)(b) and (c), which flatly prohibit selling in any channel other than the AUTHORIZED CHANNEL OF TRADE and make such sales a terminable breach. Whether a pre-existing account is protected or a breach would have to be construed.

The paragraph declares that "there exists no relationship of any kind, contractual or otherwise, between Ind.Distr. and Kellogg" even though Exhibit C is itself an instrument signed by Kellogg and the independent distributor. The qualifier "except to the extent expressly set forth herein" leaves the scope of that disclaimed relationship uncertain.

The acknowledgment permits Kellogg's direct sales to the independent distributor's customers only "to the extent permitted by the agreement then in effect between Kellogg and Premier," which points back to Sections 3(i), 3(ii)(d) and 3(ii)(k) of this Agreement. What those provisions permit is itself contested, so the exhibit's limit is only as clear as they are.

Whether a statement expands Kellogg's warranty is left to be "determined by Kellogg in its sole and absolute discretion," so the prohibited conduct is defined by one party's later say-so. The independent distributor cannot know in advance what is forbidden.

Exhibit C makes its terms prevail over any inconsistent agreement between the independent distributor and Premier, while Section 15(vii) declares this Agreement, with its exhibits, the entire agreement between COMPANY and DISTRIBUTOR. Which instrument controls where Exhibit C's terms cut across DISTRIBUTOR's rights under Section 15(ii)(a) to use subdistributors would have to be construed.
